1.description: This plan teaches believers to understand the genuine, biblical condition of every person before Christ — examining Scripture’s teaching regarding humanity’s lost state, God’s gracious pursuit of the lost through common grace and conviction, and practical wisdom for cultivating genuine, gospel-centered compassion toward those who do not yet know Christ.
1.rootScripture: “And you He made alive, who were dead in trespasses and sins.” — Ephesians 2:1
1.lecture: Before any person can rightly appreciate the good news of the gospel, they must first understand the genuinely bad news it answers. Scripture’s honest diagnosis of the human condition apart from Christ is not merely that people are imperfect or in need of self-improvement, but that they are spiritually dead — separated from God, under His righteous judgment, and utterly unable to rescue themselves through effort, religion, or good behavior. Understanding this pre-salvation condition rightly is not meant to produce despair, but genuine clarity — clarity that makes the gospel’s actual rescue comprehensible and precious rather than a vague, sentimental offer. This plan explores what Scripture teaches about the lost condition, how God graciously pursues the lost even before conversion through common grace, creation’s testimony, and the Spirit’s conviction, why human effort alone can never close this gap, and how believers can cultivate genuine, patient compassion for those still in this condition throughout ongoing life and witness.
modules: Why the Lost Cannot Save Themselves
Living With Compassion for the Lost

1.1.title: Dead in Trespasses and Sins
1.1.quote: “And you He made alive, who were dead in trespasses and sins.” — Ephesians 2:1

qa.q: Why does Paul’s specific description — genuine spiritual “death,” not merely weakness or sickness — reveal that the pre-salvation condition is far more serious than mere moral imperfection requiring gradual correction?
qa.a: Paul’s specific description reveals a condition more serious than moral imperfection, since genuine death, not weakness, establishes this severe reality, meaning the pre-salvation condition represents actual spiritual death, not merely correctable weakness, but this passage’s specific language particularly requiring recognition of death’s total, comprehensive severity as the honest, biblical description of every person’s condition apart from Christ’s own, gracious intervention and regenerating work.

qa.q: How does understanding this death as total, not partial, explain why no amount of human effort, willpower, or religious activity can produce spiritual life, since dead things cannot make themselves alive through their own, internal effort?
qa.a: Understanding this death as total explains the insufficiency of human effort, since dead things cannot selfresurrect through internal effort, meaning no amount of willpower or religious activity can produce genuine spiritual life, but this passage’s honest description requiring recognition that only an external, divine act — not internal human striving — can genuinely address this condition of total spiritual death.

1.1.distinction: Describing this condition as spiritual death does not mean unbelievers are incapable of any genuine kindness, morality, or civic good; it means that, however genuinely good such actions may be, they cannot produce the spiritual life only God can grant.
reflection: Before I was saved, did I understand my condition as merely “needing improvement,” or as this passage’s genuine spiritual death?
How does this honest description change the way I think about someone I know who does not yet know Christ?
Have I ever unintentionally suggested to someone that their own effort could close this gap?
What comfort does it bring me to know my own rescue was never dependent on my own, internal effort?
How can I hold this honest diagnosis without treating unbelievers as somehow less human or less valuable?
assignment: Read Ephesians 2:1-3 and reflect on the honest, comprehensive description of spiritual death.
Identify a specific way you have witnessed this condition, without judgment, in someone’s life.
Write a short paragraph describing your own, pre-salvation condition in this passage’s honest terms.
Discuss with your peer guide how understanding this diagnosis shaped their own gratitude for grace.
Pray specifically for someone you know who remains in this condition, asking God for their genuine rescue.

1.2.title: Separated from God by Sin
1.2.quote: “But your iniquities have separated you from your God; and your sins have hidden His face from you.” — Isaiah 59:2

qa.q: Why does this passage’s specific language — sin genuinely “separating” and “hiding” God’s face — reveal that the presalvation condition involves genuine relational rupture, not merely abstract, impersonal guilt requiring legal correction alone?
qa.a: This passage’s specific language reveals genuine relational rupture, since separating and hiding describe actual, personal estrangement, meaning the pre-salvation condition specifically involves this relational rupture, not merely abstract guilt, but this passage’s specific language particularly requiring recognition of this personal, relational estrangement as characteristic of humanity’s actual, genuine separation from God prior to Christ’s reconciling work.

qa.q: How does understanding this separation as genuinely relational, not merely legal, explain why the gospel’s solution must also be relational — restoring fellowship, not merely erasing a legal record — as this passage’s language of hidden “face” specifically suggests?
qa.a: Understanding this separation as relational explains why the solution must also be relational, since restoring fellowship differs from merely erasing a legal record, meaning the gospel’s genuine solution restores actual relationship, not merely legal status alone, but this passage’s language of God’s hidden “face” particularly requiring this relational understanding throughout believers’ comprehension of both the problem and its genuine, comprehensive solution.

1.2.distinction: Emphasizing relational separation does not mean the legal dimension of sin — genuine guilt requiring atonement — becomes unimportant; rather, both dimensions, relational and legal, are genuinely true together within Scripture’s comprehensive description of the fall.
reflection: Have I understood my pre-salvation condition as merely legal guilt, without this passage’s relational dimension?
How does thinking of sin as relational separation, not just legal violation, change how I understand salvation?
What does it mean to me that God’s “face” was hidden, and now, in Christ, is genuinely turned toward me?
How might this relational understanding shape how I talk about salvation with someone who feels distant from God?
What relationship in my own life could help me understand this kind of genuine, painful separation?
assignment: Read Isaiah 59:1-2 and reflect on sin’s genuine, relational separation from God.
Consider a relationship in your own life marked by genuine estrangement, and reflect on that pain.
Write about how understanding salvation as relational restoration, not merely legal pardon, affects your gratitude.
Discuss with your peer guide how they explain this relational dimension to someone unfamiliar with the gospel.
Pray for someone who feels far from God, that they would experience genuine, restored relationship in Christ.

1.3.title: Under the Wrath and Judgment of God
1.3.quote: “He who does not believe is condemned already… and he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abides on him.” — John 3:18, 36

qa.q: Why does this passage’s sobering language — wrath already “abiding” on the unbeliever — reveal that the presalvation condition involves genuine, present exposure to God’s righteous judgment, not merely a future, distant possibility unrelated to a person’s current, actual standing?
qa.a: This passage’s sobering language reveals present exposure to judgment, since wrath already “abiding” establishes this current, not merely future reality, meaning the pre-salvation condition specifically involves this present exposure to genuine, righteous judgment, not remaining a distant future possibility alone, but this passage’s sobering language particularly requiring recognition of this present, actual reality throughout believers’ comprehension of the lost condition’s genuine, current severity and urgency.

qa.q: How does this sobering reality provide genuine, appropriate urgency for evangelism, since understanding a person’s actual, present exposure to judgment differs significantly from viewing their unbelief as merely a philosophical preference with no genuine, present consequence?
qa.a: This sobering reality provides genuine, appropriate urgency, since present exposure differs from merely philosophical preference without consequence, meaning believers should feel this passage’s genuine urgency for evangelism, not treating unbelief as merely preference, but recognizing genuine, present consequence throughout their motivation for sharing the gospel with those who remain in this condition.

1.3.distinction: Recognizing God’s genuine wrath does not mean approaching the lost with harsh, condemning judgment ourselves; it means recognizing the genuine stakes with the same seriousness Scripture itself uses, while extending the same patient compassion Christ Himself modeled toward sinners.
reflection: Have I softened or avoided this sobering reality because it feels uncomfortable to discuss?
How does understanding someone’s present, not merely future, exposure to judgment affect my urgency to share the gospel?
Do I hold this truth with appropriate seriousness while avoiding harsh, condemning judgment of my own?
What has kept me from having an urgent, genuine gospel conversation with someone I care about?
How can I communicate this sobering reality with both honesty and genuine compassion together?
assignment: Read John 3:16-18, 36 and reflect on the present, sobering reality of wrath abiding on unbelief.
Identify one specific person whose lost condition requires this renewed sense of urgency in your own heart.
Pray specifically for this person, asking God for boldness to have an honest gospel conversation.
Discuss with your peer guide how they hold urgency and compassion together in evangelism.
Journal about your own gratitude that this wrath no longer abides on you, through Christ.

2.1.title: Common Grace: God’s Kindness to All
2.1.quote: “For He makes His sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.” — Matthew 5:45

qa.q: Why does Jesus’s specific description — sun and rain given to both “evil” and “good” alike — reveal that God graciously extends genuine kindness to all people, including those still in their lost condition, not reserving His goodness exclusively for believers?
qa.a: Jesus’s specific description reveals God’s genuine kindness extended to all, since sun and rain given to both evil and good establishes this comprehensive grace, meaning God graciously extends this kindness even to those in their lost condition, not reserving goodness exclusively for believers, but this passage’s specific description particularly requiring recognition of this common grace as genuine, though distinct from saving grace, throughout God’s ongoing dealing with all humanity.

qa.q: How does recognizing this common grace help believers see even the genuine goodness, beauty, and blessing in an unbeliever’s life as evidence of God’s own, patient kindness rather than evidence that they need no genuine rescue?
qa.a: Recognizing common grace helps believers see genuine goodness as evidence of God’s patient kindness, since even unbelievers’ blessings flow from this gracious source, meaning believers should see this goodness as testimony to God’s patience, not evidence that rescue is unnecessary, but understanding this passage’s common grace as genuinely different from, though related to, the saving grace still needed by every person remaining in their lost condition.

2.1.distinction: Recognizing common grace does not mean unbelievers are therefore already right with God through their experience of His general kindness; common grace restrains evil and provides genuine blessing, but only saving grace, received through faith in Christ, actually reconciles a person to God.
reflection: Have I recognized God’s common grace at work in the life of someone who does not yet know Christ?
How does understanding this distinction — common grace versus saving grace — clarify what someone still needs?
What genuine goodness have I observed in an unbeliever’s life that reflects God’s patient kindness?
How might recognizing common grace help me approach unbelievers with greater warmth, not suspicion?
Who in my life has experienced clear common grace, and how could I point them toward saving grace as well?
assignment: Read Matthew 5:43-45 and reflect on God’s genuine kindness extended to all people.
Identify a specific way you have seen common grace at work in an unbeliever’s life this week.
Write about the distinction between common grace and saving grace in your own words.
Discuss with your peer guide how recognizing common grace shapes their own approach to evangelism.
Thank God specifically for a way His common grace has been evident in your own community.

2.2.title: General Revelation: Creation Testifies to God
2.2.quote: “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament shows His handiwork.” — Psalm 19:1

qa.q: Why does this passage’s specific declaration — creation itself “declaring” God’s glory — reveal that every person, even before hearing the gospel explicitly, has genuine access to some knowledge of God through what has been made?
qa.a: This passage’s specific declaration reveals genuine access to knowledge of God through creation, since creation “declaring” His glory establishes this available testimony, meaning every person, even before explicit gospel proclamation, has this genuine, though limited, access to knowledge of God’s existence and glory, but this passage’s specific declaration particularly requiring recognition of this general revelation as genuine, though ultimately insufficient for salvation, testimony available throughout all creation and humanity.

qa.q: How does recognizing this general revelation explain both humanity’s genuine accountability before God — since this testimony leaves no one entirely without knowledge — and the ongoing necessity of the specific, gospel message that general revelation alone cannot provide?
qa.a: Recognizing general revelation explains both genuine accountability and gospel necessity, since accountability without excuse and gospel necessity coexist, meaning humanity remains genuinely accountable given this available testimony, while still genuinely needing the specific gospel message this general revelation alone cannot provide, following this passage’s specific declaration that establishes both truths together throughout believers’ understanding of humanity’s condition and need.

2.2.distinction: Affirming general revelation does not mean creation alone is sufficient for salvation; it means people are genuinely without excuse for unbelief while still genuinely needing the specific, saving message of the gospel that only special revelation — Scripture and gospel proclamation — can provide.
reflection: Have I recognized creation’s testimony as genuine evidence of God, even before someone hears the gospel explicitly?
How does understanding general revelation change how I think about someone who has never heard the gospel?
What has creation itself taught me about God’s glory, power, and character?
How can I use creation’s testimony as a natural starting point in conversation with an unbeliever?
Why is general revelation alone insufficient, and how does this motivate my own evangelism?
assignment: Read Psalm 19:1-4 and Romans 1:19-20 and reflect on creation’s genuine testimony to God.
Spend time outdoors this week intentionally reflecting on creation’s testimony to God’s glory.
Write about how you might use this testimony as a natural starting point in a gospel conversation.
Discuss with your peer guide how general revelation and special revelation work together in evangelism.
Pray for someone who has had limited gospel exposure, that creation would prepare their heart for the message.

2.3.title: The Holy Spirit’s Convicting Work
2.3.quote: “And when He has come, He will convict the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment.” — John 16:8

qa.q: Why does Jesus’s specific promise — the Spirit’s own work to “convict” — reveal that the actual work of drawing someone toward genuine repentance belongs to God Himself, not merely to a believer’s own persuasive skill or argument?
qa.a: Jesus’s specific promise reveals conviction as God’s own work, since the Spirit’s promised conviction establishes this divine, not merely human, agency, meaning the actual work of drawing someone toward repentance belongs genuinely to God Himself, not merely to a believer’s persuasive skill, but this passage’s specific promise particularly requiring recognition of the Spirit’s genuine, prior work throughout every person’s journey toward conviction and eventual, genuine repentance and faith.

qa.q: How does recognizing this Spirit-driven conviction free believers from the crushing pressure of believing they alone must produce someone’s conversion, allowing them instead to speak faithfully while trusting God’s own, genuine work in the hearer’s heart?
qa.a: Recognizing this Spirit-driven conviction frees believers from crushing pressure, since trusting God’s work differs from believing they alone produce conversion, meaning believers should release this false burden, speaking faithfully while trusting the Spirit’s genuine, ongoing work, not carrying the impossible weight of producing conviction themselves, but resting in this passage’s promise throughout their own, faithful witness and evangelistic effort.

2.3.distinction: Trusting the Spirit’s convicting work does not mean believers should be passive or careless in how they share the gospel; it means faithful, clear proclamation is still genuinely required, even while the actual conviction and conversion remain God’s own, sovereign work.
reflection: Have I carried false pressure believing I alone must produce someone’s conversion through my own persuasion?
How does trusting the Spirit’s genuine, convicting work change the pressure I feel in gospel conversations?
Have I witnessed the Spirit’s conviction at work in someone’s life, even before they fully responded?
What would it look like to speak faithfully while genuinely trusting God with the actual outcome?
How can I remain diligent and clear in my witness while releasing this false, personal burden?
assignment: Read John 16:7-11 and reflect on the Holy Spirit’s own, promised work of conviction.
Identify a specific gospel conversation where you carried unnecessary pressure for the outcome.
Pray specifically, releasing this pressure and trusting the Spirit’s genuine work in a person’s heart.
Discuss with your peer guide how trusting the Spirit’s work has freed their own evangelism.
Journal about resting in this truth as you continue faithfully sharing the gospel with others.

3.1.title: The Insufficiency of Good Works
3.1.quote: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8-9

qa.q: Why does Paul’s specific, comprehensive denial — salvation being “not of works,” lest anyone should “boast” — reveal that good works, however genuinely valuable, can never provide the actual rescue humanity’s lost condition genuinely requires?
qa.a: Paul’s specific, comprehensive denial reveals good works’ insufficiency, since salvation being “not of works” excludes boasting, establishing this comprehensive exclusion, meaning good works, however genuinely valuable, cannot provide the actual rescue this condition requires, but this passage’s specific denial particularly requiring recognition of grace, not works, as the sole means by which genuine rescue is provided throughout Scripture’s comprehensive teaching regarding salvation.

qa.q: How does this insufficiency explain why sincere, religious effort — attempting to earn favor through moral striving — ultimately fails to address the actual, spiritual death Module 1 described, since dead people cannot produce the life only grace provides?
qa.a: This insufficiency explains why religious effort ultimately fails, since dead people cannot produce life through moral striving alone, meaning sincere religious effort, however genuine, cannot address actual spiritual death, but this passage’s specific teaching requiring recognition that only grace, not works, can genuinely address the condition this entire plan has explored throughout its comprehensive examination of humanity’s lost state.

3.1.distinction: Denying salvation by works does not mean good works are unimportant after salvation; genuine good works flow naturally from grace received, but they can never be the basis on which that grace is first received.
reflection: Have I ever relied, even subtly, on my own good works to feel secure before God?
How does understanding grace as entirely apart from works change how I approach someone trying to “be good enough”?
What religious effort have I witnessed in someone’s life that ultimately failed to provide genuine peace?
How can I explain this distinction clearly to someone who believes their good outweighs their bad?
What genuine gratitude does this passage produce in me regarding my own, unearned salvation?
assignment: Read Ephesians 2:8-10 and reflect on grace, not works, as the sole basis for salvation.
Identify someone relying on their own goodness, and pray for an opportunity to gently share this truth.
Write a clear, simple explanation of why works cannot save, to use in future gospel conversations.
Discuss with your peer guide a time they had to unlearn a works-based approach to salvation.
Journal about your own, genuine gratitude for grace received apart from any of your own works.

3.2.title: The Bondage of the Will to Sin
3.2.quote: “Most assuredly, I say to you, whoever commits sin is a slave of sin.” — John 8:34

qa.q: Why does Jesus’s specific description — sin producing genuine “slavery,” not merely occasional misstep — reveal that the lost condition involves a genuine bondage of the will, not simply isolated, correctable choices a person could freely reverse through effort alone?
qa.a: Jesus’s specific description reveals genuine bondage, since sin producing slavery, not occasional misstep, establishes this comprehensive captivity, meaning the lost condition involves this genuine bondage of the will, not merely isolated, correctable choices, but this passage’s specific description particularly requiring recognition of sin’s enslaving power as characteristic of the actual, comprehensive condition every person experiences apart from Christ’s own, liberating work and grace.

qa.q: How does recognizing this bondage explain why willpower alone, however genuinely sincere, consistently fails to produce lasting freedom, since a slave cannot free themselves through mere determination without an external, liberating rescue?
qa.a: Recognizing this bondage explains willpower’s consistent failure, since a slave cannot self-liberate through mere determination, meaning sincere willpower alone consistently fails to produce lasting freedom, but this passage’s specific teaching requiring recognition that only Christ’s own, external, liberating work can genuinely free a person from this comprehensive bondage that sin’s actual, enslaving power produces throughout the human condition.

3.2.distinction: Recognizing sin’s bondage does not mean people bear no genuine responsibility for their choices; Scripture holds both truths together — genuine bondage and genuine responsibility — without treating either as canceling the other.
reflection: Have I experienced this kind of bondage — genuinely wanting to change, yet unable to through willpower alone?
How does recognizing sin’s enslaving power change how I view someone caught in a destructive pattern?
What false confidence in willpower alone have I carried, either for myself or in how I’ve counseled others?
How does Christ’s liberating work differ from merely offering better advice or moral encouragement?
Who do I know who might need to hear that genuine freedom, not just better effort, is what they actually need?
assignment: Read John 8:31-36 and reflect on sin’s genuine bondage and Christ’s promised, liberating freedom.
Identify an area where you once experienced this kind of bondage before genuine freedom in Christ.
Write about the difference between willpower-based change and Christ’s liberating, transformative work.
Discuss with your peer guide how they explain this bondage to someone trapped in destructive patterns.
Pray for someone currently caught in this kind of bondage, that they would find genuine freedom in Christ.

3.3.title: Religion Without Regeneration
3.3.quote: “This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me.” — Matthew 15:8

qa.q: Why does Jesus’s specific criticism — honoring with lips while the heart remains genuinely “far” — reveal that religious activity itself, without genuine regeneration, can leave a person’s actual, lost condition completely untouched and unaddressed?
qa.a: Jesus’s specific criticism reveals religious activity’s potential insufficiency, since honoring with lips while the heart stays far establishes this genuine disconnect, meaning religious activity itself, without genuine regeneration, can leave the lost condition entirely unaddressed, but this passage’s specific criticism particularly requiring recognition that outward religious performance never substitutes for the genuine, inward transformation only regeneration provides throughout a person’s actual, spiritual condition and standing before God.

qa.q: How does understanding this distinction help believers discern when someone’s religious activity, however sincere or extensive, may still leave them genuinely unconverted, requiring gentle, honest gospel conversation rather than assumed spiritual safety based on outward practice alone?
qa.a: Understanding this distinction helps discern genuine unconversion despite religious activity, since sincere religious practice does not guarantee genuine regeneration, meaning believers should discern this possibility gently and honestly, not assuming spiritual safety based on outward practice alone, but pursuing this passage’s called-for discernment throughout their gospel conversation with religiously active, yet possibly unconverted, individuals.

3.3.distinction: Recognizing this danger does not mean judging every religiously active person as unconverted; it means genuine gospel conversation, not assumption either way, is warranted whenever someone’s actual, inward relationship with Christ remains unclear.
reflection: Have I ever assumed someone’s genuine salvation based merely on their outward, religious activity?
Do I understand the difference between outward religious performance and genuine, inward regeneration?
Have I ever mistaken my own religious activity for genuine relationship with Christ, at any point in my life?
How could I gently, honestly explore this distinction with someone whose heart status seems unclear?
What genuine evidence of regeneration, beyond mere activity, should I look for in my own life and others’?
assignment: Read Matthew 15:7-9 and reflect on the danger of outward religion without genuine, inward regeneration.
Identify a specific, gentle way to explore this distinction with someone whose spiritual status seems unclear.
Examine your own life honestly for any area where activity has substituted for genuine relationship.
Discuss with your peer guide how they discern this distinction with wisdom and grace, not harsh judgment.
Pray for discernment and gentleness as you navigate these conversations with religiously active people.

4.1.title: Seeing People as God Sees Them
4.1.quote: “But when He saw the multitudes, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd.” — Matthew 9:36

qa.q: Why does this passage’s specific description — Jesus genuinely “moved with compassion,” not merely informed or aware — reveal that the appropriate response to humanity’s lost condition is genuine, felt compassion, not merely detached, theological awareness?
qa.a: This passage’s specific description reveals genuine, felt compassion as appropriate response, since Jesus being “moved,” not merely aware, establishes this emotional, genuine reality, meaning believers should cultivate this same, genuine compassion, not remaining confined to merely detached, theological awareness, but pursuing this passage’s specific example of felt compassion as characteristic of Christ’s own, genuine heart toward the lost throughout His earthly ministry and believers’ own, continued witness.

qa.q: How does seeing people the way Jesus saw them — as genuinely “weary and scattered,” not as problems, projects, or statistics — reshape the manner in which believers approach evangelism, moving from obligation toward genuine, compassionate love?
qa.a: Seeing people as Jesus saw them reshapes evangelism’s manner, since genuine compassion differs from treating people as problems or statistics, meaning believers should cultivate this same, compassionate vision, not approaching evangelism as merely obligatory task, but pursuing this passage’s modeled, compassionate love as genuine motivation throughout their ongoing witness and engagement with those still in their lost condition.

4.1.distinction: Cultivating genuine compassion does not mean avoiding honest conversation about sin and judgment; it means holding this honesty together with the same, genuine tenderness Christ Himself modeled toward those He came to seek and save.
reflection: Do I genuinely feel compassion for the lost, or has my understanding remained merely theological and detached?
Have I ever treated evangelism as an obligation or project rather than genuine, compassionate love for a person?
How does seeing someone as “weary and scattered,” not merely as a project, change how I approach them?
Who in my life could I begin viewing through this lens of genuine, Christlike compassion this week?
How can I hold honest truth about sin together with this same, genuine tenderness Christ modeled?
assignment: Read Matthew 9:35-38 and reflect on Jesus’s own, genuine compassion for the lost multitudes.
Identify someone you have viewed as a project rather than a genuinely loved person, and pray for this to change.
Spend time this week genuinely listening to and caring for this person, without an evangelistic agenda alone.
Discuss with your peer guide how they cultivate genuine, ongoing compassion for the lost in their own life.
Journal about your own growth in seeing people the way Christ genuinely sees them.

4.2.title: Praying for the Unsaved in Your Life
4.2.quote: “Brethren, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for Israel is that they may be saved.” — Romans 10:1

qa.q: Why does Paul’s specific example — his own, genuine “heart’s desire and prayer” for the unsaved — reveal that consistent, specific intercession represents necessary, ongoing practice for believers genuinely concerned with the lost condition of specific people in their lives?
qa.a: Paul’s specific example reveals consistent intercession as necessary practice, since his genuine heart’s desire and prayer establishes this personal, ongoing pattern, meaning believers genuinely concerned with the lost should practice this same, consistent intercession, not remaining confined to occasional or vague concern, but pursuing this passage’s specific example of ongoing, personal prayer as necessary practice throughout their genuine care for specific, unsaved individuals in their own lives.

qa.q: How does praying by name, consistently, for specific unsaved individuals shift genuine concern from passive worry into active, ongoing spiritual engagement that God specifically invites and honors throughout Scripture’s teaching regarding prayer?
qa.a: Praying by name shifts concern from passive worry into active engagement, since consistent, named prayer differs from passive worry, meaning believers should practice this active, specific engagement, following Paul’s own, specific example, not remaining confined to passive worry, but pursuing this passage’s called-for, active prayer as genuine, spiritual engagement God specifically invites throughout believers’ ongoing intercession for the unsaved people in their lives.

4.2.distinction: Praying for the unsaved does not replace the need to actually speak with them; it is a necessary complement to, not substitute for, the actual gospel conversations this plan’s other lessons have addressed.
reflection: Do I currently pray specifically, by name, for the unsaved people in my life, or does my concern remain vague?
What would it look like to develop Paul’s own kind of consistent, genuine “heart’s desire and prayer” for someone?
Who are three specific, unsaved people I could commit to praying for regularly over the coming months?
How might sustained, specific prayer change my own heart and readiness to actually speak with these people?
What has prevented me from praying as consistently as I know I genuinely should for the lost?
assignment: Read Romans 10:1-4 and reflect on Paul’s own, genuine, ongoing prayer for the unsaved.
Write down the names of three specific, unsaved people in your life.
Commit to praying for these three people by name, consistently, over the next month.
Discuss with your peer guide how sustained prayer has shaped their own evangelism and compassion.
Journal about any changes in your own heart toward these specific people as you continue this practice.

4.3.title: A Lifetime of Gospel-Centered Compassion
4.3.quote: “I am debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to wise and to unwise.” — Romans 1:14

qa.q: What is the ultimate posture believers are meant to carry throughout their entire lives regarding this genuine understanding of humanity’s lost condition?
qa.a: A sustained, lifelong commitment to understanding the genuine severity of the lost condition without despair, recognizing God’s gracious pursuit through common grace, general revelation, and the Spirit’s conviction, understanding why human effort alone can never provide rescue, and cultivating genuine, Christlike compassion — not obligation — for every person who remains in this condition throughout every season of ongoing life and witness.

qa.q: Why must this understanding remain an ongoing, lifelong posture rather than doctrine learned once and then set aside without continued, compassionate application throughout believers’ daily life and relationship?
qa.a: Because new people, in this same genuine condition, will continue crossing believers’ paths throughout every season of ongoing life, this understanding necessarily requires continued, compassionate application throughout an entire lifetime, not doctrine set aside once learned, but requiring this ongoing, genuine compassion and readiness throughout believers’ continued, daily witness and relationship with those still without Christ.

4.3.distinction: Carrying this lifelong posture does not mean every interaction becomes a forced evangelistic transaction; it means genuine, patient love that remains ready, in season and out, to speak the truth this entire plan has explored whenever the door genuinely opens.
reflection: How has my understanding of the pre-salvation condition — its severity, God’s pursuit, my own responsibility — changed through this study?
What has been the most significant truth I have learned about humanity’s genuine, lost condition apart from Christ?
What specific practice from this plan do I want to carry forward as a lifelong habit of gospel-centered compassion?
What would it look like to still carry this same, genuine compassion decades from now, in every season of life?
How has this study shaped your overall commitment to those who do not yet know Christ?
assignment: Read Romans 1:14-16 once more, reflecting on Paul’s own, lifelong sense of debt and compassion.
Write a summary of the most important lesson you learned in this entire plan.
Identify one specific practice from this plan you will commit to as a lifelong habit.
Share your growth with your peer guide, along with continued areas for growth and prayer.
Write a closing prayer committing to a lifetime of gospel-centered compassion for the lost in every season ahead.

2.description: This plan teaches believers to understand the genuine, biblical person and work of Jesus Christ — examining Scripture’s teaching regarding His full deity and full humanity, His atoning death and bodily resurrection, His titles and roles, and practical wisdom for worshiping and following Him wholly throughout ongoing faith and discipleship.
2.rootScripture: “Jesus said to him, ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.’” — John 14:6
2.lecture: Every dimension of the Christian faith ultimately rests on who Jesus Christ actually is and what He actually accomplished. Scripture presents Him as no mere teacher or moral example, but the eternal Son of God who took on genuine humanity, lived a sinless life, died a substitutionary death for sin, rose bodily from the grave, ascended to the Father’s right hand, and now reigns as Lord over all creation. Understanding Christ rightly requires holding together truths that can feel paradoxical to human reason — fully God and fully man, humble servant and reigning King, crucified and risen — without diminishing either side of these genuine, biblical realities. This plan explores the person of Christ, the completed work of Christ, His various titles and roles throughout Scripture, and practical wisdom for responding to who He genuinely is through worship and wholehearted discipleship throughout ongoing faith and life.
modules: The Titles and Roles of Christ

1.1.title: Fully God, Fully Man
1.1.quote: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” — John 1:14

qa.q: Why does John’s specific declaration — the eternal “Word” genuinely becoming “flesh” — reveal that Christ is authentically both fully God and fully man together, not merely appearing human while remaining only divine, nor a lesser being somewhere between the two?
qa.a: John’s specific declaration reveals Christ as authentically both fully God and fully man, since the eternal Word genuinely becoming flesh establishes this dual, complete reality, meaning Christ is neither merely appearing human nor a lesser, intermediate being, but this passage’s specific declaration particularly requiring recognition of this genuine, dual nature as central, biblical truth regarding Christ’s actual, complete person throughout Scripture’s consistent testimony and the church’s historic confession.

qa.q: How does holding both natures together — without diminishing either His genuine deity or His genuine humanity — provide the necessary foundation for understanding why Christ alone could accomplish the atonement Module 2 will explore, since only a genuinely human sacrifice could represent humanity, and only a genuinely divine sacrifice could satisfy infinite justice?
qa.a: Holding both natures together provides necessary foundation for the atonement, since only genuine humanity can represent humanity while only genuine deity can satisfy infinite justice, meaning this dual nature is not abstract theological curiosity but the actual, necessary foundation for Christ’s atoning work, requiring both genuine humanity and genuine deity together as this passage’s declaration specifically establishes throughout Scripture’s teaching regarding Christ’s complete, necessary person.

1.1.distinction: Affirming both natures does not mean Christ was partly God and partly man, as though divided; historic Christian teaching affirms He is fully, completely both at once, two natures united in one person, a genuine mystery to be believed, not fully explained by human reason.
reflection: Have I tended to emphasize Christ’s deity while neglecting His genuine humanity, or the reverse?
How does understanding both natures together deepen my appreciation for what Christ actually accomplished?
What comfort do I find in knowing Christ genuinely experienced human life, including its genuine limitation and suffering?
What confidence do I find in knowing this same Christ is genuinely, fully God?
How would I explain this dual nature simply to someone encountering this truth for the first time?
assignment: Read John 1:1-14 and reflect on the eternal Word genuinely becoming flesh.
Identify one passage emphasizing Christ’s deity and one emphasizing His genuine humanity, and compare them.
Write a simple, two-sentence explanation of Christ’s dual nature you could share with someone else.
Discuss with your peer guide how they hold both truths together in their own understanding and worship.
Journal about your own worship deepening as you consider both Christ’s deity and humanity together.

1.2.title: The Eternal Son
1.2.quote: “He is before all things, and in Him all things consist.” — Colossians 1:17

qa.q: Why does Paul’s specific description — Christ existing “before all things” — reveal that the Son’s existence is genuinely eternal, not beginning at Bethlehem, but existing eternally alongside the Father before creation itself came into being?
qa.a: Paul’s specific description reveals the Son’s genuinely eternal existence, since existing “before all things” establishes this pre-creation reality, meaning Christ’s existence did not begin at Bethlehem, but this passage’s specific description particularly requiring recognition of His genuine, eternal existence alongside the Father, not a created being with a beginning, throughout Scripture’s consistent testimony regarding the Son’s eternal, uncreated nature and being.

qa.q: How does this eternal existence provide important foundation for understanding the incarnation as the eternal Son genuinely entering time and taking on flesh, not a new being coming into existence, but this passage’s eternal Son adding genuine humanity to His already-existing, eternal person?
qa.a: This eternal existence provides important foundation for understanding the incarnation, since the eternal Son entering time differs from a new being coming into existence, meaning the incarnation represents this eternal Son genuinely adding humanity, not beginning to exist, but this passage’s specific declaration particularly requiring this understanding throughout believers’ comprehension of the incarnation’s genuine, theological significance and meaning.

1.2.distinction: Affirming the Son’s eternal existence does not diminish the genuine reality of the incarnation; rather, it makes the incarnation more remarkable still — the eternal, uncreated Son genuinely, humbly entering the limitation of human, created existence.
reflection: Have I understood Christ’s existence as beginning at His birth, rather than this passage’s revelation of eternal, prior existence?
How does recognizing this eternal existence deepen my appreciation for the humility of the incarnation?
What does it mean to me that the One who created all things chose to enter His own creation as a human being?
How might this truth shape my own worship of Christ as genuinely, eternally divine?
What questions do I still have about how to understand this eternal, yet incarnate, reality?
assignment: Read Colossians 1:15-17 and John 1:1-3 and reflect on Christ’s genuine, eternal existence.
Write about the remarkable humility this eternal existence reveals regarding the incarnation.
Reflect on this truth in worship this week, considering the eternal Son’s humble entrance into creation.
Discuss with your peer guide how this truth shapes their own understanding of Christ’s person.
Journal about your own, deepened worship considering Christ’s eternal, yet humbly incarnate, existence.

1.3.title: Christ’s Sinless Life
1.3.quote: “For we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but was in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin.” — Hebrews 4:15

qa.q: Why does this passage’s specific qualifier — genuinely tempted “as we are,” yet “without sin” — reveal that Christ’s sinlessness was not merely theoretical or automatic, but genuinely tested and proven through real, human temptation and experience?
qa.a: This passage’s specific qualifier reveals genuinely tested sinlessness, since tempted “as we are, yet without sin” establishes real, proven experience, meaning Christ’s sinlessness was not merely theoretical or automatic, but genuinely tested through real temptation, but this passage’s specific qualifier particularly requiring recognition of this proven, experienced sinlessness as characteristic of Christ’s genuine, complete human experience throughout His earthly life and ministry.

qa.q: How does this proven sinlessness qualify Christ uniquely to serve as the sacrifice Module 2 will explore, since only a genuinely sinless offering could atone for sin without also needing atonement for its own, personal guilt?
qa.a: This proven sinlessness qualifies Christ uniquely as sacrifice, since a sinless offering, unlike any other, requires no atonement of its own, meaning Christ’s genuine, proven sinlessness is not incidental detail but this passage’s necessary qualification for His unique role as sacrifice, without which His death could not accomplish the atoning work this plan’s second module will specifically explore and explain throughout Scripture’s teaching.

1.3.distinction: Affirming Christ’s sinlessness does not mean His temptations were somehow unreal or less difficult than ours; Scripture presents His temptation as genuinely real and difficult, making His sinless response all the more remarkable, not less significant.
reflection: Have I understood Christ’s sinlessness as merely automatic, rather than this passage’s genuinely tested, proven reality?
How does knowing Christ was genuinely tempted, yet without sin, provide comfort in my own struggles with temptation?
What difference does it make that my High Priest genuinely understands, from real experience, what temptation feels like?
How does this proven sinlessness deepen my appreciation for what His sacrifice actually accomplished?
In what current struggle could I draw specific comfort from Christ’s own, genuine understanding of temptation?
assignment: Read Hebrews 4:14-16 and reflect on Christ’s genuinely tested, proven sinlessness.
Identify a current struggle where you could draw comfort from Christ’s genuine understanding.
Bring this specific struggle to God in prayer, drawing on this passage’s promise of sympathetic help.
Discuss with your peer guide how Christ’s proven sinlessness has shaped their own confidence in His sacrifice.
Journal about the comfort and confidence this truth provides for your own, ongoing struggle with temptation.

2.1.title: His Substitutionary Death
2.1.quote: “He Himself bore our sins in His own body on the tree.” — 1 Peter 2:24

qa.q: Why does Peter’s specific language — Christ genuinely bearing “our sins,” not merely suffering alongside us — reveal that His death was an actual, substitutionary exchange, not merely an example of suffering or solidarity with human pain?
qa.a: Peter’s specific language reveals an actual substitutionary exchange, since Christ genuinely bearing “our sins,” not merely suffering alongside, establishes this exchange, meaning His death represents this actual, substitutionary reality, not merely an example, but this passage’s specific language particularly requiring recognition of this genuine exchange — our sin, His bearing of it — as characteristic of Scripture’s consistent teaching regarding Christ’s actual, atoning death and its genuine significance for sinners.

qa.q: How does this substitutionary understanding provide the actual, specific content behind saying “Jesus died for me,” moving this from a vague, sentimental phrase into concrete, understood exchange that genuinely addresses the lost condition this plan’s companion study has explored?
qa.a: This substitutionary understanding provides concrete content behind “Jesus died for me,” since concrete exchange differs from vague sentiment, meaning believers should understand this exchange specifically, not leaving the phrase vague, but grasping this passage’s concrete, substitutionary content as the actual, genuine reality behind Christ’s death addressing humanity’s genuine, lost condition throughout Scripture’s comprehensive teaching regarding atonement.

2.1.distinction: Understanding Christ’s death as substitutionary does not mean this is the only genuine dimension of the atonement Scripture describes; substitution stands alongside other genuine truths — victory over evil, example of love — without any of these canceling or replacing the others.
reflection: Have I understood “Jesus died for me” as a vague, sentimental phrase rather than this passage’s concrete, substitutionary reality?
How does understanding this actual exchange — my sin, His bearing of it — deepen my gratitude and worship?
What specific sin in my own life do I find comfort knowing was genuinely borne by Christ on my behalf?
How would I explain this substitutionary exchange clearly to someone unfamiliar with this teaching?
What emotions arise in me as I consider this specific, costly exchange made genuinely on my behalf?

Write a clear, concrete explanation of substitutionary atonement in your own words.

2.2.title: His Bodily Resurrection
2.2.quote: “But now Christ is risen from the dead, and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” — 1 Corinthians 15:20

qa.q: Why does Paul’s specific description — Christ as the “firstfruits” of resurrection — reveal that His resurrection was genuinely bodily and historical, establishing the actual pattern and guarantee for believers’ own, future resurrection rather than remaining merely symbolic or spiritual?
qa.a: Paul’s specific description reveals genuinely bodily, historical resurrection, since “firstfruits” establishes an actual pattern guaranteeing a future harvest, meaning Christ’s resurrection was genuinely bodily and historical, not merely symbolic, but this passage’s specific description particularly requiring recognition of this bodily reality as establishing the actual, guaranteed pattern for believers’ own future resurrection throughout Scripture’s comprehensive teaching regarding this central, historical event.

qa.q: How does this resurrection provide the actual, historical vindication that Christ’s claims and sacrifice were genuinely accepted by God, functioning as proof rather than mere postscript to the story told throughout Module 2’s exploration of His completed work?
qa.a: This resurrection provides actual, historical vindication, since proof differs from mere postscript, meaning the resurrection functions as this passage’s genuine, historical proof that Christ’s claims and sacrifice were accepted by God, not remaining a mere addendum, but standing as necessary, evidential vindication throughout believers’ confident understanding of Christ’s completed, genuine work and accomplished salvation.

2.2.distinction: Affirming the bodily resurrection does not mean the resurrected body was identical in every way to His pre-death, earthly body; Scripture describes a genuinely transformed, yet genuinely physical, body — the same pattern promised for believers’ own future resurrection.
reflection: Have I treated the resurrection as merely a symbolic ending to the story, rather than this passage’s genuine, historical vindication?
How does understanding the resurrection as historical proof strengthen my own confidence in the gospel’s truth?
What hope do I draw from the promise that my own resurrection will follow this same, “firstfruits” pattern?
How would I explain the resurrection’s evidential significance to someone skeptical of its historical reality?
What questions do I still have about the nature of the resurrected, yet still physical, body?

2.3.title: His Ascension and Present Reign
2.3.quote: “So then, after the Lord had spoken to them, He was received up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God.” — Mark 16:19

qa.q: Why does this passage’s specific description — Christ genuinely “received up” and now seated at God’s “right hand” — reveal that His work did not conclude with the resurrection, but continues in His present, active reign and ongoing ministry?
qa.a: This passage’s specific description reveals continued, ongoing work, since being genuinely received up and seated establishes present, active reign, meaning Christ’s work did not conclude at the resurrection, but this passage’s specific description particularly requiring recognition of His present, active reign and continued ministry — including His ongoing intercession — as characteristic of Christ’s genuine, present position throughout believers’ understanding of His complete, comprehensive work.

qa.q: How does understanding Christ’s present, active reign — not mere absence or distance — provide genuine comfort and confidence for believers navigating present, ongoing difficulty, since this passage reveals He is genuinely, actively reigning, not merely remembered from a completed, past story?
qa.a: Understanding Christ’s present, active reign provides genuine comfort, since present, active reign differs from mere absence or distant memory, meaning believers navigating present difficulty should draw on this passage’s revelation of genuine, ongoing reign, not treating Christ as merely a past, completed story, but recognizing His present, active involvement throughout their ongoing life and continued relationship with Him.

2.3.distinction: Affirming Christ’s present reign does not mean His physical absence is unimportant or without genuine significance; His bodily ascension establishes genuine, physical absence from earth even while His authority and active involvement remain genuinely, presently active through the Holy Spirit and His ongoing intercession.
reflection: Have I thought of Christ’s work as concluded at the resurrection, rather than this passage’s continued, present reign?
How does understanding Christ’s active, present reign provide comfort in a specific difficulty I currently face?
What does it mean to me that Christ is genuinely, actively interceding for me right now?
How does this present reign shape my confidence regarding the future, not merely the past events of the gospel?
What would it look like to more intentionally draw on this present reign throughout my daily life this week?

3.1.title: Christ as Savior
3.1.quote: “For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.” — Luke 2:11

qa.q: Why does this angelic announcement’s specific title — “Savior,” announced at Christ’s very birth — reveal that rescue, not merely instruction or example, was genuinely central to His mission from its earliest, announced beginning?
qa.a: This angelic announcement’s specific title reveals rescue as genuinely central from the start, since “Savior,” announced at birth, establishes this mission’s core purpose from its earliest beginning, meaning rescue, not merely instruction, was genuinely central to Christ’s mission, but this passage’s specific title particularly requiring recognition of this saving purpose as central, not incidental, to understanding who Christ actually is and why He genuinely came throughout Scripture’s consistent testimony regarding His mission.

qa.q: How does embracing Christ specifically as Savior require believers to acknowledge their own, genuine need for rescue, since a savior is only meaningful to someone who recognizes they cannot save themselves, connecting directly to this plan’s earlier exploration of humanity’s lost condition?
qa.a: Embracing Christ as Savior requires acknowledging genuine need for rescue, since a savior is only meaningful to someone recognizing their inability to self-save, meaning believers must genuinely acknowledge this need, not approaching Christ as merely helpful example, but recognizing this passage’s title as requiring honest acknowledgment of the lost condition this rescue specifically, genuinely addresses throughout believers’ understanding of who Christ actually is for them.

3.1.distinction: Calling Christ “Savior” does not mean His role is limited to a single, past moment of rescue; His ongoing work of saving — sanctifying and preserving believers — continues throughout their entire, ongoing life and journey of faith.
reflection: Have I approached Christ primarily as a helpful teacher, rather than genuinely, personally as my Savior?
What does it mean to me, specifically, that I genuinely needed rescue, not merely instruction or example?
How does understanding Christ’s ongoing saving work — not just a past moment — shape my daily dependence on Him?
What area of my life do I currently need to genuinely entrust to Christ as Savior, not merely admire from a distance?
How would I explain to someone why “Savior” is a more accurate title than merely “good teacher” or “example”?

Identify a current area of life where you need to more genuinely entrust yourself to Christ as Savior.

Journal about your own, ongoing dependence on Christ’s continued, saving work throughout your life.

3.2.title: Christ as Lord
3.2.quote: “That if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.” — Romans 10:9

qa.q: Why does Paul’s specific pairing — confessing Jesus as “Lord,” alongside genuine belief — reveal that genuine faith includes submission to Christ’s actual authority, not remaining confined to intellectual agreement alone without this genuine, submitted allegiance?
qa.a: Paul’s specific pairing reveals faith’s inclusion of submission, since confessing “Lord” alongside belief establishes this necessary allegiance, meaning genuine faith includes this submission to Christ’s actual authority, not remaining confined to intellectual agreement alone, but this passage’s specific pairing particularly requiring recognition of “Lord” as necessary confession alongside belief, characteristic of genuine, complete, saving faith throughout Scripture’s teaching regarding authentic conversion and continued discipleship.

qa.q: How does acknowledging Christ as Lord require ongoing, practical surrender of specific areas of life — finances, relationships, ambition — rather than a one-time, verbal confession disconnected from actual, continued obedience and submission?
qa.a: Acknowledging Christ as Lord requires ongoing, practical surrender, since actual obedience differs from disconnected verbal confession, meaning believers should pursue this ongoing, practical surrender of specific life areas, not remaining confined to one-time confession alone, but embracing this passage’s called-for lordship as requiring genuine, continued obedience throughout their ongoing, daily life and relationship with Christ as genuine Lord, not merely acknowledged Savior.

3.2.distinction: Acknowledging Christ’s lordship does not mean achieving perfect, immediate obedience in every area; it means a genuine, ongoing posture of submission and growth, even amid continued struggle and incomplete surrender in specific areas still being worked out.
reflection: Have I confessed Christ as Savior while withholding genuine submission to Him as Lord in specific areas of my life?
What specific area of my life — finances, relationships, ambition — do I still struggle to genuinely surrender to Christ?
How does understanding lordship as ongoing surrender, not one-time confession, change how I approach obedience?
What would it look like to take one, specific step of surrender in this area this week?
How can I hold genuine grace for incomplete surrender while still pursuing this ongoing posture of submission?
assignment: Read Romans 10:9-10 and reflect on confessing Christ as Lord alongside genuine belief.
Identify one specific area of your life requiring greater, practical surrender to Christ’s lordship.
Take one concrete step of surrender in this specific area this week.
Discuss with your peer guide how they have grown in surrendering specific areas to Christ’s lordship over time.
Journal about your own, ongoing journey of surrender as you continue growing under Christ’s genuine lordship.

3.3.title: Christ as the Coming King
3.3.quote: “Behold, He is coming with clouds, and every eye will see Him.” — Revelation 1:7

qa.q: Why does John’s specific promise — Christ genuinely returning, visible to “every eye” — reveal that His current, hidden reign will one day give way to genuinely visible, universal recognition of His kingship over all creation?
qa.a: John’s specific promise reveals a future, visible transition, since Christ’s return being visible to “every eye” establishes this genuine, universal recognition, meaning His current, hidden reign will one day become visible and universally acknowledged, but this passage’s specific promise particularly requiring recognition of this coming, visible reality as characteristic of believers’ genuine, biblical hope regarding Christ’s promised, future return and comprehensive reign over all creation.

qa.q: How does this future hope shape believers’ present life, providing genuine motivation for faithful endurance and holy living now, since present circumstances, however difficult, are genuinely temporary compared to this passage’s promised, coming reality?
qa.a: This future hope shapes present life, since temporary present circumstances differ from this promised, coming reality, meaning believers should draw genuine motivation from this future hope, enduring faithfully and living in holiness now, not remaining discouraged by present, temporary circumstance, but anchoring their present life in this passage’s promised, coming reality throughout their ongoing faith and continued, faithful endurance.

3.3.distinction: Anticipating Christ’s coming reign does not mean withdrawing from present, faithful engagement with the world; genuine hope in His return should motivate greater, not lesser, faithfulness in present responsibility and witness.
reflection: How often do I genuinely consider Christ’s promised, future return in my present, daily thinking and life?
How does this future hope provide motivation for faithful endurance in a current difficulty I am experiencing?
Have I ever used this future hope as an excuse for present withdrawal, rather than genuine, faithful engagement?
What would it look like to live with greater, present faithfulness because of this coming, promised reality?
How does anticipating “every eye” seeing Him shape how I think about my own, present witness and life?
assignment: Read Revelation 1:7 and Titus 2:11-13 and reflect on the promised, coming return of Christ as King.

Reflect on how this hope should shape greater present engagement, not withdrawal, from your responsibilities.

4.1.title: Worshiping Christ Rightly
4.1.quote: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and riches and wisdom, and strength and honor and glory and blessing!” — Revelation 5:12

qa.q: Why does this passage’s comprehensive declaration — Christ genuinely “worthy” of power, riches, wisdom, and glory — reveal that worship is the appropriate, comprehensive response to everything this plan has explored regarding His person and completed work?
qa.a: This passage’s comprehensive declaration reveals worship as the appropriate, comprehensive response, since Christ’s genuine worthiness across every category establishes this fitting response, meaning worship represents the appropriate, comprehensive response to His person and work, not remaining confined to merely intellectual assent, but this passage’s comprehensive declaration particularly requiring genuine, comprehensive worship as characteristic of appropriate response throughout believers’ ongoing relationship with Christ and understanding of His genuine worth.

qa.q: How does genuine worship require both understanding — the theological content this plan has explored — and heartfelt response, since worship divorced from genuine understanding becomes empty emotion, while understanding divorced from genuine response remains incomplete, cold theology?
qa.a: Genuine worship requires both understanding and heartfelt response, since worship without understanding becomes empty emotion while understanding without response remains cold theology, meaning believers should hold both dimensions together, not settling for either alone, but pursuing this passage’s comprehensive, both intellectually grounded and genuinely felt worship throughout their ongoing relationship with and response to Christ’s genuine person and worth.

4.1.distinction: Worshiping Christ rightly does not require identical, uniform emotional experience in every moment; genuine worship includes both seasons of strong feeling and seasons of quiet, faithful acknowledgment of truth, both genuinely valid expressions of the same, underlying worship.
reflection: Has my worship of Christ remained merely intellectual, or merely emotional, without this passage’s called-for combination?
How has this entire study deepened both my understanding and my genuine, felt worship of who Christ actually is?
What specific truth from this plan has most moved me toward genuine, heartfelt worship?
How can I hold both understanding and feeling together in my ongoing worship, not settling for either alone?
What would it look like to worship Christ more intentionally, both privately and corporately, this week?

Discuss with your peer guide how their understanding of Christ has deepened their own, genuine worship.

4.2.title: Following Christ Wholly
4.2.quote: “Then Jesus said to His disciples, ‘If anyone desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me.’” — Matthew 16:24

qa.q: Why does Jesus’s specific instruction — genuine self-denial and cross-bearing — reveal that following Him wholly requires comprehensive, costly commitment, not merely admiring His teaching from a comfortable, unaffected distance?
qa.a: Jesus’s specific instruction reveals comprehensive, costly commitment, since genuine self-denial and cross-bearing establish this necessary cost, meaning following Christ wholly requires this comprehensive commitment, not merely admiring His teaching from a distance, but this passage’s specific instruction particularly requiring this costly, genuine following as characteristic of authentic discipleship throughout believers’ ongoing relationship with and response to who Christ genuinely is and requires.

qa.q: How does this comprehensive following flow naturally from everything this plan has explored — His genuine person, completed work, and rightful titles — rather than representing an additional, separate requirement disconnected from genuine understanding of who Christ actually is?
qa.a: This comprehensive following flows naturally from everything explored, since genuine understanding naturally produces this response, not a separate requirement, meaning wholehearted discipleship represents the natural, appropriate response to genuinely understanding Christ’s person and work, not remaining a disconnected, additional requirement, but flowing from this passage’s called-for following as appropriate response throughout believers’ comprehensive, genuine relationship with Christ as Savior, Lord, and coming King.

4.2.distinction: Following Christ wholly does not mean achieving flawless, complete discipleship from the outset; it means a genuine, ongoing direction and posture of following, even while continued growth, struggle, and dependence on grace remain part of this lifelong journey.
reflection: Have I admired Christ’s teaching from a comfortable distance without genuinely following Him wholly?
What specific area of self-denial does this passage’s instruction bring to mind for my own life right now?
How does everything I’ve learned throughout this plan about Christ’s person and work shape my willingness to follow Him?
What would wholehearted, costly following look like practically in my current circumstances?
How can I hold genuine grace for my incomplete discipleship while still pursuing this ongoing, wholehearted following?

Identify one specific area of self-denial you sense Christ is calling you toward right now.
Take a concrete step in this specific area this week, trusting Christ’s grace throughout the process.
Discuss with your peer guide how they have grown in wholehearted following over their own journey.
Journal about your own, ongoing commitment to follow Christ wholly, not merely admire Him from a distance.

4.3.title: A Lifetime of Knowing Christ
4.3.quote: “That I may know Him and the power of His resurrection.” — Philippians 3:10

qa.q: What is the ultimate posture believers are meant to carry throughout their entire lives regarding this significant, comprehensive understanding of who Jesus Christ actually is?
qa.a: A sustained, lifelong commitment to knowing Christ ever more deeply — His full deity and humanity, His completed, atoning work, His present reign, and His promised return — responding with genuine worship and wholehearted, costly following throughout every season of ongoing faith, understanding, and discipleship.

qa.q: Why must this understanding remain an ongoing, lifelong pursuit rather than truth learned once and then set aside without continued, growing knowledge of Christ throughout believers’ ongoing spiritual life?
qa.a: Because Christ’s own, infinite person and work continue providing genuine depth for growing knowledge throughout every season of ongoing life, this understanding necessarily requires continued, deliberate pursuit throughout an entire lifetime, not truth learned once and then set aside, but requiring this ongoing, deepening knowledge and worship throughout believers’ entire, continuing life and relationship with Christ.

4.3.distinction: Committing to this lifelong pursuit does not mean arriving at complete, exhaustive knowledge of Christ in this present life; the lifelong journey includes continued growth and discovery, with sustained, faithful pursuit of everdeepening knowledge being the genuine, ongoing goal.
reflection: How has my understanding of Christ’s person and work — His deity, humanity, completed work, titles — deepened through this study?
What has been the most significant truth I have learned about who Jesus Christ genuinely is throughout this study?

What would it look like to still be growing in this knowledge decades from now, in every season of my life?
How has this study shaped your overall commitment to knowing and following Christ throughout your continuing journey?

3.description: This plan teaches believers to understand the genuine, biblical gospel in its full, comprehensive content — examining the bad news it honestly answers, the good news it actually proclaims, its universal scope for all people, and practical wisdom for guarding and sharing this gospel throughout ongoing life and witness.
3.rootScripture: “For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that He was buried, and that He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures.” — 1 Corinthians 15:3-4
3.lecture: The gospel is not a vague feeling of religious inspiration but specific, historical, defined content — the same content Paul says he “received” and faithfully “delivered” to others. Understanding the gospel rightly requires holding together its honest diagnosis of humanity’s genuine condition and its equally genuine, historical solution accomplished through Christ’s death and resurrection. This gospel is not a message reserved for the especially religious or morally impressive; it genuinely levels every person, offering the same rescue to all who will receive it by grace through faith. Because this gospel is precious and easily distorted, believers must also learn to guard it against subtle additions or subtractions that would turn good news into another burden to carry. This plan explores the gospel’s bad news and good news, its universal reach, and practical wisdom for guarding and sharing this unchanging message throughout ongoing life and witness.

1.1.title: The Reality of Sin
1.1.quote: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23

qa.q: Why does this passage’s comprehensive statement — “all have sinned,” without exception — establish sin as universal reality requiring genuine acknowledgment before the gospel’s good news can be rightly understood or received?
qa.a: This passage’s comprehensive statement establishes sin as universal, since “all have sinned” admits no exception, meaning genuine acknowledgment of this universal reality is necessary before the gospel’s good news can be rightly understood, but this passage’s specific, comprehensive language requiring this honest acknowledgment as foundational to any accurate presentation of the gospel’s actual, complete message.

qa.q: How does understanding sin as falling short of God’s own glory, not merely breaking arbitrary rules, reveal the actual, relational nature of the offense every person’s sin represents against a genuinely holy God?
qa.a: Understanding sin as falling short of God’s glory reveals its relational, not merely rule-based, nature, since falling short of glory describes an offense against a person, not merely a rule, meaning sin’s genuine offense is fundamentally against God Himself, not merely impersonal regulation, but this passage’s language particularly requiring this personal, relational understanding of sin’s true, comprehensive nature.

1.1.distinction: Naming sin’s universal reality does not mean every sin carries identical, practical consequence in this life; it means every person, without exception, genuinely stands in need of the same rescue this plan goes on to describe.
reflection: Have I minimized sin as merely breaking rules, rather than this passage’s revelation of falling short of God’s glory?
How does recognizing sin as universal change how I view both myself and every other person I encounter?
What personal example of falling short of God’s glory, not merely a rule, comes to mind for me honestly?
How would I explain sin’s relational, not merely legal, nature to someone unfamiliar with this teaching?
How does this honest diagnosis prepare me to actually appreciate the good news that follows?

4.description: This plan teaches believers to understand the genuine, biblical response the gospel requires — examining Scripture’s teaching regarding repentance, faith, and confession as the actual, necessary components of genuine conversion, and practical wisdom for making this response real throughout ongoing life and continued relationship with Christ.
4.rootScripture: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand. Repent, and believe in the gospel.” — Mark 1:15
4.lecture: Understanding the gospel’s content is not the same as genuinely responding to it. Scripture consistently pairs two essential responses — repentance and faith — as the necessary, God-enabled human response to the good news of Christ’s death and resurrection. This response involves genuine turning from sin, genuine trust in Christ alone, and genuine, open confession of who He is. This is not a mechanical transaction completed by reciting particular words, but an actual, heartfelt turning of the whole person toward God. This plan explores what genuine repentance and saving faith actually involve, why confession and surrender matter, and practical wisdom for making this response real — through prayer, through telling someone, and through ongoing, lifelong response — throughout continued life and relationship with Christ.
